content: When a person experiences getting the wind knocked out of them, it refers to a temporary spasm of the diaphragm. This occurs when a sudden force is applied to the abdomen, exerting pressure on the solar plexus. The result is a transient paralysis of the diaphragm, making it difficult to breathe for a short period of time. This phenomenon can also occur from a strong blow to the back. When the abdomen is struck, a significant pressure difference is created across the diaphragm. This causes the diaphragm to stretch, which in turn stretches the nerves associated with the diaphragm. The mechanical force from this stretching induces a muscle spasm in the diaphragm, similar to the sensation of a charley horse in the leg. It typically takes a few seconds for the diaphragm to relax and for normal breathing to resume. In martial arts, practitioners are often trained to exhale forcefully when struck in the stomach. This technique helps to minimize the effects of such a spasm. During a diaphragm spasm, the laryngeal muscles may also contract, producing an inspiratory sound known as stridor. This sound can be heard for several breathing cycles as normal respiration is restored. Another example of a diaphragm spasm is singultus, more commonly referred to as hiccups. However, hiccups are a much milder form of diaphragm spasm. During a hiccup episode, voluntary control of breathing is briefly impaired, but only for a fraction of a second (measured in milliseconds), as opposed to the several seconds of impairment seen when the wind is knocked out of someone.
